1.pericope_label: And Sarah was an hundred and seven and twenty years old: these were the years of the life of Sarah. And Sarah died in Kirjath–arba; the same is Hebron in the land of Canaan: and Abraham came to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her.

schools.summary: Note the singularity that Sarah alone among women has her age, death and burial recorded, and assign the reason — the honour was hers as ancestress of the Hebrew race; take Kirjath-arba literally as the City of Four and pair it with the meaning of Hebron, alliance, so that the town looks founded by a union of four families and Arba is a personal name taken from the city rather than the reverse; then move past the mourning to the next act, Abraham rising from before his dead to approach the Hittites as lords and possessors of the city.

Attend to the Hebrew, which repeats the word years after each numeral, and use it to dismiss the rabbinic reading that made Sarah as beautiful at a hundred as at twenty, since such repetition is simply usual in the language; canvass the Jewish etymologies of Kirjath-arba and prefer the one that makes Arba a great man among the Anakim; and reason carefully from the word came that Abraham was not present at the death, rejecting the notion that a few tents' distance could account for it.

Remark that no other woman in the sacred writings has her age, death and burial so distinctly noted, and enlarge the honour by way of Paul, who makes Sarah a type of the Church and celebrates her faith in the promise of a son; then answer the difficulty of Abraham's coming practically, from the twenty-four miles between Beersheba and Hebron and the temporary residences a man keeps for his flocks; and insist that the two verbs mark real lamentation, not merely the customary ceremonies.

Take the number as a memento rather than a fact, since Sarah had called herself old forty years before, and draw the moral that reckoning ourselves old makes us die not the sooner but the better, the longest liver dying at last and the special favourites of Heaven not exempted; then make the mourning a duty, picturing Abraham sitting by the body that his eye might affect his heart, tears being a tribute due to our friends, though not the sorrow of those without hope.

debates.question: Why is Sarah's age recorded when no other woman's is?

sides.position: Because she was deemed worthy of higher honour, Paul making her a type of the Church and celebrating her faith in the promise of a son
Because the honour was hers as ancestress of the Hebrew race
As a memento of mortality, since she had called herself old forty years before

debates.question: Where does the name Kirjath-arba come from?

sides.position: From the four Anakim who lived there, or from the four couples buried there
From Arba, a great man among the Anakim
From a Canaanite chief who had three brothers
From a union of four families founding the town, Arba being a personal name taken from the city
Not to be decided, the matter not being necessary to be known

debates.question: Why does Moses say Abraham came to mourn for Sarah?

sides.position: Because they were not living together: more likely their dwelling was at Hebron or the vale of Mamre, and a few tents' distance will not explain it
Because he had settled at Beersheba, twenty-four miles off, and kept temporary residences for his flocks
Because Isaac had been left at Hebron in charge of his mother and the cattle

outliers.note: Alone attends to the Hebrew repetition of the word years after each numeral, and uses it to dismiss the rabbinic reading that made Sarah as beautiful at a hundred as at twenty and as modest in the flower of her age as at seven.
Alone draws a rule of ageing from the number, that old people will die never the sooner but may die the better for reckoning themselves old.

3.pericope_label: And Abraham stood up from before his dead, and spake unto the sons of Heth, saying, I am a stranger and a sojourner with you: give me a possession of a buryingplace with you, that I may bury my dead out of my sight. And the children of Heth answered Abraham, saying unto him, Hear us, my lord: thou art a mighty prince among us: in the choice of our sepulchres bury thy dead; none of us shall withhold from thee his sepulchre, but that thou mayest bury thy dead.

schools.summary: Notice what the narrative omits and what it dwells on, that the burial rite is passed over while the purchase is recited at length, and turn to the custom itself as observed religiously in all ages and among all peoples — arising not from curiosity or superstition but from a natural sense God never suffered to perish, that men might witness to themselves a future life; then read the request twice over, either as humility that makes the suit likelier to succeed or as a guard against the suspicion of covetousness, and find a seed of piety in Hittites who honour gifts they know to be God's.

Take the self-description as concerning Abraham's mind rather than his circumstances, on the authority of the epistles, since he felt he had no certain dwelling place and sought by faith a city with foundations, and add that burial in another man's ground was reckoned ignominious in various nations, which may be why the offered sepulchres are declined; then draw from burying the dead out of sight that death makes unpleasant to us those who while they lived were the desire of our eyes, and mark the contrast between the stranger's self-naming and the prince the Hittites call him.

Supply the legal situation the request presupposes: strangers might pasture cattle on the open downs, but permanent occupation needed the natives' consent and appropriation required a public compact ratified by the whole tribe at the gate; order the two acts, prostration in the tent first and rising afterwards; explain prince of God as a Hebrew idiom of surpassing excellence, like the wind of God or the cedars of God; and note the commercial reality behind the courtesy, that payment was presupposed on both sides though kept in the background.

Turn the standing up into counsel for the over-grieved, who must take heed of poring on their loss and sitting alone and melancholy, since there is a time to cease mourning and the care of a funeral may divert grief where it is likeliest to tyrannise — weeping must not hinder sowing; then impute Abraham's want of a grave to God's providence rather than any improvidence of his, and wish that all who provide burying-places for their bodies were as careful to provide a resting-place for their souls.

debates.question: What does Abraham mean by calling himself a stranger and a sojourner?

sides.position: His state of mind rather than his circumstances, on the authority of the epistles: he sought by faith a city with foundations
His legal position: strangers might pasture cattle on the open downs, but permanent occupation required the natives' consent
A guard against suspicion, or simply humility that makes the suit likelier to succeed

debates.question: Why are the offered sepulchres declined?

sides.position: Because burial in another man's ground was reckoned ignominious in various nations
Because the courteous offer never meant a free sepulchre: payment was presupposed on both sides, kept in the background in Oriental fashion

outliers.note: Alone turns the purchase into an argument about burial itself, observed religiously in all ages and among all peoples, and traces it not to curiosity or superstition but to a natural sense God never suffered to perish, by which men witness to themselves a future life.
Alone reads the standing up as counsel against over-grieving, warning off poring on the loss and sitting alone and melancholy, since weeping must not hinder sowing.

themes: standing up from before the dead

7.pericope_label: And Abraham stood up, and bowed himself to the people of the land, even to the children of Heth. And he communed with them, saying, If it be your mind that I should bury my dead out of my sight; hear me, and intreat for me to Ephron the son of Zohar, That he may give me the cave of Machpelah, which he hath, which is in the end of his field; for as much money as it is worth he shall give it me for a possession of a buryingplace amongst you. And Ephron dwelt among the children of Heth: and Ephron the Hittite answered Abraham in the audience of the children of Heth, even of all that went in at the gate of his city, saying, Nay, my lord, hear me: the field give I thee, and the cave that is therein, I give it thee; in the presence of the sons of my people give I it thee: bury thy dead.

schools.summary: Ask why a free grave is refused and reject the easy answer about not being obliged in a small matter: Abraham would receive no gratuitous possession from men whom God was to eject that he might succeed them, preferring the bare promise to present dominion; treat the bowing as ordinary civil reverence, paid to men as well as to God though for a different end; leave the division of the cave an open question after canvassing the versions; and turn the insistence on paying into a rebuke of common bargaining, where the seller asks twice the worth and the buyer shuffles to bring it low.

Reconstruct the staging of the negotiation, Abraham having already seen the cave and learned whose it was, coming to the gate of Hebron where the elders sat to administer justice and where bargains were made and witnessed, and addressing them so that their influence might be used with the owner; then note the speed of the outcome, that a man who expected to have to entreat for a sale received an outright gift at the first mention; and take the whole exchange as proof that religion teaches good manners.

Read the name as an outer and an inner compartment rather than a doubled valley, and correct the English twice over: the text does not say Ephron dwelt among the Hittites but that he was sitting in their midst, every free-born citizen having the right to be present where matters were settled by common consent; and the request is not for a grave among them but that the cave be given in the midst of them, in general assembly, so that the sale be duly attested — the thrice-repeated giving being the courtly form for mutual presents.

sides.position: An outer and an inner compartment of the cavern
The valley, since the surrounding land is also called the field of Machpelah
One part above and the other below, in one version; more likely a single entrance with a middle partition within, but the question may be left open

debates.question: Why does Abraham refuse a free grave?

sides.position: So as not to be obliged in so small a matter
To receive no gratuitous possession from men whom God was to eject that he might succeed them

debates.question: Was Ephron's offer of the field a real gift?

sides.position: A courtly form only, the parties speaking as though making mutual presents rather than buying and selling
A real gift refused, since what Ephron declined was not the request but the payment
A real gift, and remarkably prompt, given at the first mention where entreaty was expected

outliers.note: Alone turns the insistence on paying into a rebuke of ordinary dealing, where the seller sets the price at twice the worth and the buyer shuffles to bring it low, and reports Abraham’s rule about gifts: he would neither receive all, nor in all things, nor from all men.
Alone makes the bowing a maxim about manners, that religion teaches good manners and those abuse it who place it in rudeness and clownishness.

themes: as much money as it is worth

12.pericope_label: And Abraham bowed down himself before the people of the land. And he spake unto Ephron in the audience of the people of the land, saying, But if thou wilt give it, I pray thee, hear me: I will give thee money for the field; take it of me, and I will bury my dead there. And Ephron answered Abraham, saying unto him, My lord, hearken unto me: the land is worth four hundred shekels of silver; what is that betwixt me and thee? bury therefore thy dead. And Abraham hearkened unto Ephron; and Abraham weighed to Ephron the silver, which he had named in the audience of the sons of Heth, four hundred shekels of silver, current money with the merchant.

schools.summary: Report the close of the bargain plainly, that Abraham agreed at once and judged the sum a moderate price between man and man; then spend the comment demolishing Jerome, who had said a letter was dropped from Ephron's name once he consented to take money, his virtue maimed by the sale of a sepulchre — the name stands written exactly as before, nor is it a fault that a man pressed to sell took the lawful price, and if there was sin here Abraham must bear the blame; and follow the mischief down to the Canonists, who made selling sepulchres sacrilege while their own clergy suffer no grave to be dug unless paid for.

Correct the version, since for if thou wilt give it we should read but if thou wilt sell it, and the keseph offered is silver rather than coined money, no such coin being probable then; price the shekel at three shillings English on Dr. Prideaux's authority rather than the common two and sixpence, making four hundred sixty pounds sterling, while insisting a weight is meant since the next verse says Abraham weighed; gloss the silver current with the merchant as passing with the traveler, what we should call a hawker or peddler; and defend the refusal of the gift as justice and prudence rather than pride.

Strip the Hebrew back — no verb of giving at all, simply but if thou wilt, I pray thee, hear me — and recover the courtliness our version misses, Ephron fixing his price only indirectly by asking what four hundred shekels is betwixt him and Abraham; read the obeisance as the Oriental method of returning thanks for a request granted; and press the point that shekel means weight and coinage came long afterwards, so that inserting the word money antedates the facts: it was the silver that was current, drawn into small bars marked by the refiner, of which some two hundred ounces were weighed out.

Make the openness of the transaction the lesson, since prudence as well as justice directs us to be fair and open in our dealings and cheating bargains will not bear the light, the money paid at once, in full, and by weight, current with the merchant and without deceit; and observe that although all Canaan was Abraham's by promise, the time of possessing it was not come, so what he had occasion for he bought and paid for — dominion is not founded in grace, and a title to an eternal inheritance neither entitles men to this world's possessions nor justifies them in doing wrong.

debates.question: What was the price in modern money?

sides.position: Sixty pounds sterling, reckoning the shekel at three shillings English on Dr. Prideaux's authority rather than the common two and sixpence
About fifty pounds, no mean price considering the high value of silver in those days

debates.question: Was Ephron's virtue diminished by accepting payment?

sides.position: Yes, and a letter was struck from his name to mark it
No: the name stands written exactly as before, and no blame attaches to a man pressed to sell who took the lawful price

outliers.note: Alone follows Jerome’s remark down to the Canonists, who made it sacrilege to sell sepulchres while the clergy of their own communion suffer no grave to be dug unless the price be paid.
Alone reconstructs the physical form of the payment, silver drawn into small bars and marked by the refiner to indicate quality, of which some two hundred ounces were weighed out.

17.pericope_label: And the field of Ephron, which was in Machpelah, which was before Mamre, the field, and the cave which was therein, and all the trees that were in the field, that were in all the borders round about, were made sure Unto Abraham for a possession in the presence of the children of Heth, before all that went in at the gate of his city. And after this, Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the cave of the field of Machpelah before Mamre: the same is Hebron in the land of Canaan. And the field, and the cave that is therein, were made sure unto Abraham for a possession of a buryingplace by the sons of Heth.

schools.summary: Work out the topography from before Mamre taken as opposite to it, placing the oak-grove on the western slope of the valley whose eastern side holds the Haram, and dismissing the tradition that puts it at Ramet-el-Chalil as neither fitting nor near enough, its supposed remains of Abraham's house being the ruins of a heathen temple; compare this legally exact document with the terra-cotta tablets of Ur-Chasdim now in our museums; and read the repetition of the conveyance as legal accuracy that measures the event's importance, a burying-place bought in strict form being proof of faith in the promises.

Call this the earliest account on record of the purchase of land and admire the simplicity and candour of both sides — the gate where justice was administered and bargains concluded, the offer of a free sepulchre out of common hospitality, the refusal, the silver weighed down, and the passers-by serving as witnesses — so that the conveyance was made sure without those puzzlers of civil affairs by whose chicanery property becomes insecure, a censure at once qualified as falling on the complexity of modern law rather than on honourable lawyers; and note that those who have least of this earth find a grave in it.

Settle the disputed name from the wording of the deed, since a field is said to be in Machpelah and a field could never be in a cave, so that Machpelah is the proper name of a tract of ground however the double cave be explained; then treat the burial itself as part of the security, Sarah's interment being possession taken for the use the ground was bought for and a pledge and earnest of the land promised to Abraham's seed; and answer the difficulty raised from Stephen's speech, that he had a possession to bury in but not to live upon, no ground of his own to till or sow or build on.

debates.question: Is Machpelah a place-name or a description?

sides.position: The proper name of a tract of ground, since the field is said to be in Machpelah and a field could never be in a cave
An appellative, the field of Ephron being rendered as in the double cave
holders: unnamed renderers (as reported by Gill, citing Vatablus)

sides.position: An appellative, but inverted to better sense so that the cave is in the field, though not agreeably to the Hebrew

debates.question: Where was Abraham's oak-grove at Mamre?

sides.position: On the western slope of the valley, opposite the Haram on its eastern side
At Ramet-el-Chalil, which neither fits the description nor is near enough, its supposed remains of Abraham's house being a heathen temple
holders: old Christian tradition (as reported by Ellicott)

outliers.note: Alone compares this legally exact document with the terra-cotta tablets now in our museums which record the daily business of the people of Ur-Chasdim, the city Abraham had left.
Alone turns the witnessed conveyance into a complaint against modern law, whose accumulation and complexity puzzle justice herself, while carefully exempting honourable lawyers from the censure.
